explanations.explanation: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, writes that Jesus "…considered me faithful and appointed me to service." Look at who is doing the considering: Jesus, not Paul. Paul isn't bragging about his résumé here. He's saying thank you, and I'd be thanking Him too.

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, doesn't thank Jesus for making him famous. The word he uses is "faithful." Jesus considered him faithful and appointed him to service. Nobody needs a fan club for that, friend.
No money in this verse, friend. Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, says Jesus considered him "faithful" and appointed him to service. That's the thing he's thankful for.
Paul says it plainly: "…I was shown mercy." Blasphemer, persecutor, violent man, and still mercy. That's the whole point of the verse. Mercy shows up right where you'd least expect it.
You'd think that's where this list was headed, wouldn't you? But Paul says the opposite: "…I was shown mercy." He says it right after naming his past. Judgment isn't the word he lands on.
A warning would have been fair, but that's not what Paul writes. He says he "…was shown mercy." The list of his old ways ends with mercy, not a lecture.

Paul says he "…had acted in ignorance and unbelief…" Then he adds that he was shown mercy. He's not making excuses for the blasphemy, the persecuting and the violence. He's just telling us how it was, and that mercy found him anyway.
Paul actually says the opposite. In 1 Timothy 1:13 he writes that he "…had acted in ignorance and unbelief…" That's the way he describes his persecuting days. And mercy came to him right there.

Paul says the grace of our Lord overflowed to him, "…along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus." Grace didn't show up by itself. It brought faith and love with it. That's some serious gift wrapping.

Paul never lists riches or honor here. He says grace overflowed to him "…along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus." Those two came with the grace. And you can't put faith and love in a cookie jar, though I've tried.

Joy and peace sound lovely, but they aren't the pair in this verse. Paul says grace overflowed "…along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus." Faith and love are the two riding along with it. Joy and peace never get a mention, friend.

explanations.answer: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners
explanations.explanation: Paul calls this saying trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance. Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. That's the saying, short and sweet.

explanations.answer: Christ Jesus came into the world to reward the good
explanations.explanation: That one flips the saying around. Paul says Christ Jesus came "…to save sinners…" Look at how Paul describes himself right alongside it, and you can see why that saying is good news for him. It's good news for everybody who needs saving.

explanations.answer: Christ Jesus came into the world to rebuild the temple
explanations.explanation: No temple in this saying, friend. Paul says Christ Jesus came into the world "…to save sinners…" That's the saying he calls trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance. It's about people being saved.

Paul says Christ Jesus came to save sinners, "…of whom I am the worst." He doesn't dodge it or soften it. Then in the next verse he tells us why mercy found him. If the worst can be saved, nobody's too far gone.
Paul doesn't pick "wisest." He says he is "the worst." Ouch, right? He's talking about himself, and he says it plainly (1 Timothy 1:15). Nobody's handing out a trophy for that one.
Age doesn't come up here. Paul writes that he is "the worst" of the sinners Christ Jesus came to save. That's a pretty honest thing to say about yourself. Even I wouldn't say that on a résumé.

explanations.answer: So Jesus could display His patience as an example
explanations.explanation: Paul writes that he was shown mercy "…so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life." So Paul himself is the example. If Jesus can be that patient with him, there's hope for everybody who comes after.

explanations.answer: So Paul could prove he had kept the law
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say a word about proving anything. He says he was shown mercy so Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example. The mercy was about Jesus' patience, not Paul's record. Good thing, because Paul just called himself the worst.

explanations.answer: So the churches would no longer fear him
explanations.explanation: The churches don't come up in this verse at all. Paul says he was shown mercy so that Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example. That's the reason he gives, and he gives no other.
Paul says Jesus displayed His "perfect patience" with him. Perfect, not just enough to get by. So that statement has it backwards, friend.
Paul writes that Christ Jesus displayed "…His perfect patience…" That's not a little, and it's not just enough to get by. It's complete. Paul is the example of it.

Paul says Jesus' patience with him is "…an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life." Eternal life is what those believers are trusting Him for. If He was that patient with Paul, He can be patient with whoever believes in Him.

Good health is a fine thing to have, but it's not what Paul says here. He says the example is for "…those who would believe in Him for eternal life." That's what believers are trusting Him for in this verse.
No treasure chest in this verse, friend. Paul says it's an example to "…those who would believe in Him for eternal life." Eternal life is the thing here. Riches don't even get a mention.
Paul praises "…the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God…" Eternal means no ending. He adds, "…be honor and glory forever and ever." So this King doesn't pass away.

Paul calls Him "…the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God…" Eternal and immortal mean this King doesn't pass away. And Paul says honor and glory belong to Him "…forever and ever." Amen!

Paul writes to Timothy, whom he calls his child, that the command is "…in keeping with the previous prophecies about you, so that by them you may fight the good fight…" So the prophecies are there to help him in that fight. That's some real backup.

Paul doesn't ask Timothy, whom he calls his child, to settle every argument. He says the prophecies are there so that by them Timothy "…may fight the good fight…" That's the job, and no one has to win every argument to do it.
Nothing about leaving here. Paul tells Timothy, whom he calls his child, that by the previous prophecies about him he "…may fight the good fight…" That's the purpose Paul gives, plain and simple.

explanations.answer: By holding on to faith and a good conscience
explanations.explanation: Paul tells Timothy to fight the good fight "…holding on to faith and a good conscience…" So the way to fight is to hold on. I'll take a firm grip any day, especially when the dough gets slippery.

explanations.answer: By holding on to the law and the temple
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say a word about the law or the temple here. He says to fight the good fight "…holding on to faith and a good conscience…" Those are the two things to keep a grip on.

explanations.answer: By holding on to his rights and his reputation
explanations.explanation: That's a lot to hold with only two hands, and Paul doesn't ask Timothy to hold either one. He says to fight the good fight "…holding on to faith and a good conscience…" That's the grip that counts.

Paul tells Timothy to hold on to faith and a good conscience, "…which some have rejected and thereby shipwrecked their faith." A shipwreck is a hard picture. That's the word he uses, and it's a heavy one.
It goes the other direction. Paul says of faith and a good conscience, "…which some have rejected and thereby shipwrecked their faith." Nothing got stronger there. A shipwreck is no place to be.
Hidden would be gentler than what Paul says. He says of faith and a good conscience, "…which some have rejected and thereby shipwrecked their faith." That's a ship broken up, not tucked away.
Paul names them: "Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander…" They're among those who shipwrecked their faith. Paul says he has handed them over to Satan "…to be taught not to blaspheme."
Those two aren't in this passage. The names Paul gives are Hymenaeus and Alexander. They're listed among those who shipwrecked their faith.
Not those two, friend. Paul names Hymenaeus and Alexander in this passage. Those are the two among the people who shipwrecked their faith.

Paul writes that he has "…handed over to Satan…" Hymenaeus and Alexander "…to be taught not to blaspheme." The aim he states is that they be taught. This is a heavy part of the letter, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously.

Paul really does say it. He writes that he has "…handed over to Satan…" Hymenaeus and Alexander "…to be taught not to blaspheme." The purpose he gives is that they be taught. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's one to read slowly.
